<div class="page-shell">

<header class="masthead">
  <div class="eyebrow">WebR practical</div>
  <h1>Interaction terms in linear regression</h1>
  <p>An interaction lets the effect of one predictor depend on another. Start with a binary group, extend to a categorical predictor with several levels, and finish with two continuous predictors — reading each group's own slope straight from the coefficient table.</p>
</header>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Overview</h2>

An **additive** model assumes the slope of a predictor is the same at every level of the other predictors:

```r
lm(outcome ~ x + group, data = my_data)
```

An **interaction** model lets that slope change with the other predictor. In R you write the interaction with a colon, or use `*` as shorthand for "both main effects plus their interaction":

```r
lm(outcome ~ x + group + x:group, data = my_data)
lm(outcome ~ x * group, data = my_data)          # identical to the line above
```

The whole practical rests on one skill: given the coefficient table, **work out each group's own slope**. In this practical you will:

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li>Fit a binary interaction and read the reference and non-reference slopes.</li>
  <li>Extend to a <strong>polytomous</strong> categorical predictor with three levels.</li>
  <li>Handle two <strong>continuous</strong> predictors, where the "slope" becomes a moving target.</li>
</ul>

After answering the questions, <strong>your completion code will be revealed.</strong>

</section>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 1 — A binary interaction</h2>

We ask: **does blood pressure medication change the BMI → systolic BP relationship?**

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><strong>Outcome:</strong> <code>sysbp</code> (systolic blood pressure)</li>
  <li><strong>Continuous predictor:</strong> <code>bmi</code></li>
  <li><strong>Binary predictor:</strong> <code>meds</code> (<code>noMeds</code> = reference, <code>onMeds</code>)</li>
</ul>

Run the cell to build the data and see the two groups.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: create the data and plot</h3>

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)

set.seed(42)
n <- 60
bp <- data.frame(
  bmi = round(runif(n, 20, 40), 1),
  meds = factor(rep(c("noMeds", "onMeds"), each = n / 2))
)
bp$sysbp <- with(bp, round(
  88 + 1.7 * bmi + ifelse(meds == "onMeds", 57 - 1.0 * bmi, 0) + rnorm(n, 0, 4), 1
))

ggplot(bp, aes(x = bmi, y = sysbp, color = meds)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#b83b5e", "#00565e")) +
  labs(x = "BMI", y = "Systolic BP", color = "BP meds") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 1</div>
  <p>The two fitted lines in the plot are clearly <strong>not parallel</strong>. In regression language, what does non-parallel say?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="a">The two groups have different intercepts but the same slope.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="b">BMI has no relationship with systolic BP.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="c">The slope of BMI on systolic BP differs between the two medication groups.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Non-parallel lines mean the BMI slope itself depends on medication status — that is an interaction." data-incorrect="Not quite. Different slopes (not just different heights) is exactly what an interaction means."></div>
</div>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fit the interaction model — fill in the blank</h3>

Use `*` so R adds both main effects and the interaction. Replace `____` and run.

```{webr-r}
m_int <- lm(sysbp ~ bmi ____ meds, data = bp)
round(coef(m_int), 2)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

```r
m_int <- lm(sysbp ~ bmi * meds, data = bp)
round(coef(m_int), 2)
```

You should get roughly:

```
   (Intercept)            bmi     medsonMeds  bmi:medsonMeds
         83.08           1.84          61.62          -1.10
```

</details>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Reading the two slopes</h2>

The coefficient table does not hand you each group's slope directly — you build them. The reference group (`noMeds`) uses the plain `bmi` row. The other group adds the interaction row on top.

<table class="slope-table">
  <caption>Building each group's line from the four coefficients</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Group</th><th>Intercept</th><th>BMI slope</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr class="refrow"><td>noMeds <em>(reference)</em></td><td><code>83.08</code></td><td><code>1.84</code></td></tr>
    <tr><td>onMeds</td><td><code>83.08 + 61.62 = 144.70</code></td><td><code>1.84 + (−1.10) = 0.74</code></td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

The `medsonMeds` coefficient (`+61.62`) shifts the **intercept**; the `bmi:medsonMeds` coefficient (`−1.10`) shifts the **slope**. So among people on medication, BMI is associated with a much flatter rise in systolic BP.

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 2</div>
  <p>What is the BMI slope for the <code>onMeds</code> group?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="a"><code>1.84</code> — the <code>bmi</code> row applies to everyone.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="b"><code>1.84 + (−1.10) = 0.74</code> — add the interaction row to the reference slope.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="c"><code>−1.10</code> — the interaction row is the on-meds slope.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The non-reference slope is the reference slope plus the interaction coefficient." data-incorrect="Not quite. The interaction coefficient is not a slope by itself — you add it to the reference slope."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 3</div>
  <p>Predict the systolic BP for a person <strong>on meds</strong> with BMI = 30. Use the on-meds intercept and slope from the table.</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="a"><code>144.70 + 0.74 * 30 = 166.90</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="b"><code>83.08 + 1.84 * 30 = 138.28</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="c"><code>144.70 + 1.84 * 30 = 199.90</code></label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. For the on-meds group use its own intercept (144.70) and its own slope (0.74)." data-incorrect="Not quite. Use the on-meds row: intercept 144.70 and slope 0.74, not the reference numbers."></div>
</div>

<div class="callout">
<p><strong>The interaction equation.</strong> With <code>g = 1</code> for on-meds and <code>0</code> for the reference group:</p>

$$
\widehat{\text{sysbp}} = b_0 + b_1\,\text{bmi} + b_2\,g + b_3\,(\text{bmi}\times g)
$$

<p>The reference slope is <code>b1</code>. The non-reference slope is <code>b1 + b3</code>. That single idea is all you need for the rest of the practical — the only thing that changes is how many groups (or values) there are.</p>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 2 — A polytomous categorical predictor</h2>

Now the grouping variable has **more than two levels**. Nothing new happens conceptually: R still picks one level as the reference and gives every other level its own main-effect row **and** its own interaction row.

We ask: **does the way lung function (FEV, in mL) declines with age depend on smoking history?**

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><strong>Outcome:</strong> <code>fev</code> (forced expiratory volume, mL)</li>
  <li><strong>Continuous predictor:</strong> <code>age</code> (years)</li>
  <li><strong>Categorical predictor:</strong> <code>smoking</code> with three levels — <code>never</code> (reference), <code>former</code>, <code>current</code></li>
</ul>

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: create the data and plot three groups</h3>

```{webr-r}
set.seed(7)
n2 <- 90
lung <- data.frame(
  age = round(runif(n2, 30, 70)),
  smoking = factor(rep(c("never", "former", "current"), each = 30),
                   levels = c("never", "former", "current"))
)
lung$fev <- with(lung, round(
  5200 - 20 * age +
    ifelse(smoking == "former",  -200 - 10 * age,
    ifelse(smoking == "current", -300 - 25 * age, 0)) +
    rnorm(n2, 0, 150)
))

ggplot(lung, aes(x = age, y = fev, color = smoking)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#00565e", "#f5a742", "#b83b5e")) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "FEV (mL)", color = "Smoking") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

</div>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fit the interaction — fill in the blanks</h3>

```{webr-r}
m_poly <- lm(fev ~ ____ ____ ____, data = lung)
round(coef(m_poly), 1)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

```r
m_poly <- lm(fev ~ age * smoking, data = lung)
round(coef(m_poly), 1)
```

You should get roughly:

```
       (Intercept)                age      smokingformer     smokingcurrent
            5230.7              -19.9             -280.8             -390.3
 age:smokingformer age:smokingcurrent
              -9.3              -22.9
```

</details>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Reading three slopes from one table</h2>

Same rule as before, just repeated for each non-reference level. The reference level (`never`) uses the plain `age` row. Each other level adds its own `age:smoking___` interaction row.

<table class="slope-table">
  <caption>Each smoking level gets its own intercept and its own age slope</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Group</th><th>Intercept</th><th>Age slope (mL per year)</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr class="refrow"><td>never <em>(reference)</em></td><td><code>5230.7</code></td><td><code>−19.9</code></td></tr>
    <tr><td>former</td><td><code>5230.7 + (−280.8) = 4949.9</code></td><td><code>−19.9 + (−9.3) = −29.2</code></td></tr>
    <tr><td>current</td><td><code>5230.7 + (−390.3) = 4840.4</code></td><td><code>−19.9 + (−22.9) = −42.8</code></td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

Lung function falls with age for everyone, but it falls **fastest for current smokers** (−42.8 mL/year) and slowest for those who never smoked (−19.9 mL/year).

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 4</div>
  <p>A three-level categorical predictor in an interaction model produces how many interaction rows?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="a">Three — one per level.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="b">One — a single interaction term covers the whole variable.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="c">Two — one for each non-reference level.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The reference level is the baseline; each of the other two levels gets its own main-effect row and its own interaction row." data-incorrect="Not quite. The reference level has no rows of its own — the other two levels each contribute one interaction row."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 5</div>
  <p>What is the age slope for <strong>former</strong> smokers?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="a"><code>−9.3</code> — read the <code>age:smokingformer</code> row directly.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="b"><code>−19.9 + (−9.3) = −29.2</code> — reference slope plus the former interaction row.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="c"><code>−280.8</code> — the <code>smokingformer</code> row is the slope.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Add the level's interaction coefficient to the reference age slope." data-incorrect="Not quite. The interaction row (−9.3) is only the *difference* in slope; add it to the reference slope −19.9."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 6</div>
  <p>The <code>smokingcurrent</code> coefficient is <code>−390.3</code>. What does it describe on its own?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="a">How much lower the current-smoker line sits at age = 0 (the intercept gap), not a slope.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="b">The age slope for current smokers.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="c">The predicted FEV for a current smoker of any age.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. A level's main-effect row shifts the intercept; the matching age:smoking___ row shifts the slope." data-incorrect="Not quite. The main-effect row is an intercept shift (the gap at age 0); the slope change lives in the age:smoking___ row."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 7</div>
  <p>Predict FEV for a <strong>current</strong> smoker aged 60, using the current-smoker row of the table.</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="a"><code>5230.7 + (−19.9) * 60 = 4036.7</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="b"><code>4840.4 + (−19.9) * 60 = 3646.4</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="c"><code>4840.4 + (−42.8) * 60 = 2272.4</code></label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Use the current-smoker intercept (4840.4) with the current-smoker slope (−42.8)." data-incorrect="Not quite. For a current smoker use both current-smoker numbers: intercept 4840.4 and slope −42.8."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 3 — Two continuous predictors</h2>

Now there are **no groups at all** — both predictors are continuous. The syntax is identical (`x * z`), but the interpretation gains one twist: the interaction coefficient is the change in one predictor's slope **for each one-unit increase in the other**. There is no longer a small set of groups, so instead of a group-by-group table we tabulate the slope at a few chosen values.

We ask: **does the effect of dietary sodium on systolic BP depend on age?**

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><strong>Outcome:</strong> <code>sysbp</code> (systolic BP)</li>
  <li><strong>Continuous predictor:</strong> <code>sodium</code> (g/day)</li>
  <li><strong>Continuous predictor:</strong> <code>age</code> (years)</li>
</ul>

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: create the data and fit</h3>

```{webr-r}
set.seed(99)
n3 <- 80
salt <- data.frame(
  sodium = round(runif(n3, 1.5, 5), 1),
  age = round(runif(n3, 25, 75))
)
salt$sysbp <- with(salt, round(
  95 + 2 * sodium + 0.3 * age + 0.10 * sodium * age + rnorm(n3, 0, 5), 1
))

m_cont <- lm(sysbp ~ sodium * age, data = salt)
round(coef(m_cont), 3)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>Show the answer (expected coefficients)</summary>

```
(Intercept)      sodium         age  sodium:age
     96.621       0.957       0.308       0.111
```

</details>

<section class="panel">

<h2>The slope is now a moving target</h2>

For the binary and polytomous cases, "the other group's slope = reference slope + interaction row." With two continuous predictors the same algebra holds, but "the other level" is replaced by a **value** of the second predictor. The sodium slope is:

<div class="formula-panel">

$$
\text{slope of sodium} = b_{\text{sodium}} + b_{\text{sodium:age}} \times \text{age} = 0.957 + 0.111 \times \text{age}
$$

</div>

Instead of one row per group, we read the slope off at chosen ages — the direct analogue of the group tables above:

<table class="slope-table">
  <caption>Sodium's slope on systolic BP, evaluated at several ages</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Age</th><th>Sodium slope = <code>0.957 + 0.111 × age</code></th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>30</td><td><code>0.957 + 0.111 × 30 = 4.29</code></td></tr>
    <tr><td>50</td><td><code>0.957 + 0.111 × 50 = 6.51</code></td></tr>
    <tr><td>70</td><td><code>0.957 + 0.111 × 70 = 8.73</code></td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

Salt matters more for blood pressure in older people: each extra gram of sodium is linked to a bigger BP rise as age goes up. (By symmetry, the age slope is likewise `0.308 + 0.111 × sodium` — either predictor can be read as moderating the other.)

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 8</div>
  <p>With two continuous predictors, why can't you report a single number as "the sodium slope"?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="a">Because continuous predictors have no slope.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="b">Because the sodium slope depends on age — it changes as age changes.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="c">Because the model failed to converge.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The interaction makes each predictor's slope a function of the other, so you must state at what value you are reading it." data-incorrect="Not quite. The interaction term means the sodium slope is 0.957 + 0.111 × age — a different number at every age."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 9</div>
  <p>What is the sodium slope for a 40-year-old?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="a"><code>0.957 + 0.111 * 40 = 5.40</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="b"><code>0.111 * 40 = 4.44</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="c"><code>0.957</code> — the <code>sodium</code> row is the slope at any age.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Plug age = 40 into 0.957 + 0.111 × age." data-incorrect="Not quite. Use the full expression 0.957 + 0.111 × age with age = 40. The 0.957 row alone is the slope only at age 0."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 10</div>
  <p>The <code>sodium</code> main-effect coefficient is <code>0.957</code>. At what value of age is that the actual sodium slope?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p9" value="a">At the average age in the data.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p9" value="b">At every age — it is the slope everywhere.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p9" value="c">At age = 0, where the interaction term drops out.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. A main effect in an interaction model is the slope when the other predictor is 0 — which is why centering predictors often makes it more meaningful." data-incorrect="Not quite. Set age = 0 in 0.957 + 0.111 × age and the interaction term vanishes, leaving 0.957."></div>
</div>

<div class="callout warning">
<p><strong>When should you fit an interaction?</strong> Fit one when it is your research question (does X's effect depend on Z?), when it is well established (e.g. age × sex in growth charts), or when design or biology suggests effect modification. Do <strong>not</strong> fit every pairwise interaction and keep only the significant ones — that is p-hacking and invalidates those p-values. Otherwise default to the simpler additive model: easier to read and more stable.</p>
</div>

<script>
const COMPLETION_CODE = "INT3SLOPES";
const COMPLETION_REQUIRED = 8;

function updateCompletion() {
  const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".practice");
  const correct = document.querySelectorAll(".practice.is-correct").length;
  const total = cards.length;
  const progress = document.getElementById("code-progress");
  const box = document.getElementById("code-box");
  const value = document.getElementById("code-value");

  if (progress) {
    progress.textContent = correct + " of " + total + " correct (need at least " + COMPLETION_REQUIRED + ")";
  }

  if (box && value) {
    if (correct >= COMPLETION_REQUIRED) {
      value.textContent = COMPLETION_CODE;
      box.style.display = "block";
    } else {
      box.style.display = "none";
    }
  }
}

document.querySelectorAll(".practice").forEach((card) => {
  const button = card.querySelector("button");
  const feedback = card.querySelector(".practice-feedback");
  const answer = card.dataset.answer;

  button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    const selected = card.querySelector("input[type='radio']:checked");
    card.classList.remove("is-correct", "is-incorrect");
    card.querySelectorAll("label").forEach((label) => {
      label.classList.remove("correct-choice", "incorrect-choice");
    });

    if (!selected) {
      card.classList.add("is-incorrect");
      feedback.textContent = "Choose an answer first, then check it.";
      updateCompletion();
      return;
    }

    const selectedLabel = selected.closest("label");
    const correctInput = card.querySelector(`input[value="${answer}"]`);
    const correctLabel = correctInput ? correctInput.closest("label") : null;

    if (selected.value === answer) {
      card.classList.add("is-correct");
      selectedLabel.classList.add("correct-choice");
      feedback.textContent = feedback.dataset.correct;
    } else {
      card.classList.add("is-incorrect");
      selectedLabel.classList.add("incorrect-choice");
      if (correctLabel) correctLabel.classList.add("correct-choice");
      feedback.textContent = feedback.dataset.incorrect;
    }

    updateCompletion();
  });
});

updateCompletion();
</script>
